terms.grammar: conjunctions: an alternative question, direct, or indirect with the subjunctive; utrum may be left out
evidence: Varr. RR 3.2.11: quid enim rēfert, utrum propter ovēs, an propter avēs frūctūs capiās?
Plaut. Pers. 3.1.13: utrum prō ancillā mē habēs, an prō fīliā? (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Also -ne … an and plain … an. “Or not” is necne in an indirect question, annōn in a direct one.

terms.grammar: enclitic on the first word, an before the second
evidence: Tac. Germ. 5.3: argentum et aurum propitiīne an īrātī diī negāverint dubitō

terms.grammar: conjunction, at the end of an indirect question
evidence: Ter. Heaut. 1.1.43: nunc habeam necne, incertum est (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In a direct question, annōn: Tibi ego dīcō, annōn? (Ter. And. 762).

terms.grammar: conjunctions, with the moods of sī
evidence: Phaedr. 4.22.7–8: sīve hoc ineptum sīve laudandum est opus
terms.comment: Not a question but a double condition: “whether it is this or that, the main clause holds”.

phrases.latin: quid enim rēfert, utrum propter ovēs, an propter avēs frūctūs capiās?
phrases.english: for what does it matter whether you make your profit from sheep or from birds?

phrases.latin: utrum prō ancillā mē habēs, an prō fīliā?
phrases.english: do you take me for a servant girl, or for your daughter?

phrases.latin: argentum et aurum propitiīne an īrātī diī negāverint dubitō
phrases.english: whether the gods denied them silver and gold in kindness or in anger, I cannot tell

phrases.latin: Amīcum an nōmen habeās, aperit calamitās.
phrases.english: Misfortune shows whether you have a friend or only the name of one.
Am I talking to you or not?

phrases.latin: sīve Aquilō rādit terrās seu brūma nivālem interiōre diem gȳrō trahit, īre necesse est
phrases.english: whether the north wind scours the land or midwinter drags the snowy day round its shorter circle, I have to go
